nameStory: Actinotaenium curtum doesn't have a widely-used common name, so scientists know it by its Latin name. The genus name 'Actinotaenium' comes from Greek words meaning 'ray-band,' referring to the radiating patterns you can see under a microscope. The species name 'curtum' means 'shortened' in Latin, describing this tiny organism's compact shape.
description: This isn't actually a plant at all, but a microscopic single-celled organism called a desmid that lives in freshwater. You'll never see individual Actinotaenium curtum with your naked eye - each cell is smaller than the width of a human hair. Under a microscope, it looks like a tiny green barrel or cylinder with slightly pinched sides. These little organisms are actually closer relatives to land plants than you might think, and they help make the water they live in crystal clear.

idTips.label: Microscopic size
idTips.description: Completely invisible to the naked eye - you'll need a microscope with at least 400x magnification to see individual cells

idTips.label: Barrel shape
idTips.description: Cells look like tiny green barrels or short cylinders with slightly constricted middle sections when viewed under magnification

idTips.label: Bright green color
idTips.description: Rich emerald green coloration from chloroplasts (the parts that do photosynthesis) arranged in distinctive patterns within each cell

idTips.label: Clear water habitat
idTips.description: Found floating in exceptionally clean, clear freshwater - their presence often indicates very pure water conditions

idTips.label: Smooth cell walls
idTips.description: Cell surface appears smooth and glassy under magnification, unlike some relatives that have bumpy or spiny textures

habitat: Lives in clean, nutrient-poor freshwater like pristine mountain ponds, bog pools, and the clearest sections of slow-moving streams in New England. You're most likely to find them in remote wilderness areas where water quality is exceptionally high. They thrive in soft water with low mineral content, often associated with sphagnum moss and other bog plants.

seasonality.spring: Most active as water temperatures rise and daylight increases - this is when populations grow rapidly through cell division.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm months when conditions are optimal for photosynthesis and reproduction.
seasonality.fall: Numbers may decline as water cools, but cells can still be found actively swimming in suitable habitats.
seasonality.winter: Populations persist under ice in unfrozen water, though growth slows significantly in cold temperatures.

funFact: These tiny organisms are actually accomplished architects - they build their cell walls from intricately patterned pieces of cellulose that fit together like microscopic puzzle pieces, and scientists can use these patterns like fingerprints to identify different species!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with its close relative Actinotaenium cucurbita, which has a more distinctly cucumber-like shape with more pronounced constrictions. Think of curtum as the 'stubby barrel' and cucurbita as the 'pinched cucumber' to keep them straight.
contextualKnowledge: Many people are surprised to learn that desmids like this one are not bacteria or protozoans, but are actually green algae - making them distant cousins of land plants. The beautiful geometric patterns in their cell walls have fascinated microscopists for over 150 years.
compareHints: Compared to its genus mate Actinotaenium cucurbita, this species is noticeably shorter and more barrel-shaped rather than elongated. While cucurbita looks like a tiny green cucumber with a clear waist, curtum appears more like a stubby cylinder with just a slight pinch in the middle. Both species prefer similar ultra-clean water conditions, but curtum tends to be less common overall.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative Actinotaenium curtum, this species has a more pronounced gourd-like swelling and constriction, while curtum tends to be more cylindrical with less dramatic shape variation.
